lesson.title: The Pure Food and Drug Act: Regulating What Americans Ate and Took as Medicine
lesson.summary: Signed by Theodore Roosevelt on June 30, 1906, the same day as the Meat Inspection Act, the Pure Food and Drug Act banned the interstate sale of mislabeled or adulterated food and drugs, capping years of advocacy by chemist Harvey Wiley and drawing immediate political momentum from the public uproar over Upton Sinclair's The Jungle.
lesson.body:
Concern about unsafe and fraudulently labeled food and medicine did not begin in 1906. For nearly two decades, Harvey Washington Wiley, the chief chemist of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, had campaigned for federal food safety legislation, running highly publicized experiments known as the Poison Squad in which volunteers ate meals dosed with common food preservatives and additives so investigators could study their effects on the human body. Wiley's efforts built scientific and public awareness of the problem, but for years Congress showed little urgency about turning that awareness into law.

What changed the political calculation was Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle, published in 1906. Sinclair had written the book to expose the exploitation of immigrant laborers in Chicago's meatpacking plants, but readers, including President Roosevelt, reacted far more strongly to Sinclair's descriptions of the filthy, dangerous conditions under which their meat was actually processed. Roosevelt ordered his own investigators to verify Sinclair's claims, and when they largely confirmed them, public outrage translated quickly into congressional action.

On June 30, 1906, Roosevelt signed both the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act into law. The Pure Food and Drug Act prohibited the manufacture and interstate sale of adulterated or misbranded food and drugs, requiring, among other things, that products accurately state their contents, an especially important step given how many patent medicines of the era secretly contained alcohol, opium, or cocaine. The companion Meat Inspection Act, responding directly to Sinclair's revelations, established federal inspection requirements for meatpacking plants engaged in interstate commerce, covering conditions and processes that had previously gone entirely unsupervised.

The Pure Food and Drug Act's enforcement was initially housed within Wiley's Bureau of Chemistry at the Department of Agriculture, an agency that would evolve over subsequent decades into the modern Food and Drug Administration. The 1906 law had real limitations, including weak penalties and gaps that later scandals would expose, and Congress would strengthen food and drug regulation repeatedly in the decades that followed. Even so, the act marked a genuine turning point, establishing for the first time that the federal government had both the authority and the responsibility to police what went into the food and medicine Americans consumed, a direct and lasting legacy of the muckraking journalism and consumer protection instincts at the heart of the Square Deal.
